title: "This Is Not a Course. It Is a Journey."
hook: That tic has a name Cicero knew: epanorthosis. This essay argues LLMs overuse it because their training text is full of promotional prose and RLHF rewards emphatic phrasing.
key_points: Epanorthosis is a classical figure of self-correction — deny a plain description, then substitute a grander one.
The essay's claim: overuse is a trained disposition, from promotional-heavy training text plus preference tuning that rewards confident, emphatic phrasing.
It proposes an Epanorthosis Index: the figure's density measured relative to genre-specific human baselines; left-to-right generation is only an amplifier.
First measurements on one instruction-tuned family find mis-calibration in both directions — overshooting in oratory, undershooting in informal Q&A.
A one-line instruction cut the figure by half to nearly three-quarters in Italian; an SFT adapter removed it almost entirely.
The stated target is calibration to the human rate per genre, not elimination.
content_html: You have read this sentence a thousand times: "This is not a course. It is a journey of transformation." The construction is old enough that Cicero and Quintilian catalogued it — epanorthosis, a figure of thought in which a speaker rejects a plain description and substitutes a grander one. This essay asks why language models reach for it so compulsively.
extra_html:
Where the habit comes from

The author's argument is that overuse is a trained disposition rather than an artifact of decoding. Two causes carry most of the weight: a training distribution thick with promotional prose, and preference tuning that rewards confident, emphatic phrasing. The left-to-right nature of generation gets demoted to an amplifier — it makes the pattern easy to continue, but it isn't why the model wanted it.

Measuring it, then dialing it back

To make the claim testable, the essay proposes an Epanorthosis Index: the figure's density scored against genre-specific human baselines rather than against zero. A first measurement across three sizes of one instruction-tuned family finds mis-calibration in both directions — the models overshoot in oratory (roughly twofold, nearly threefold in Italian, concentrated in the larger tiers) and undershoot in informal question-and-answer writing, while matching humans in argument, journalism, and encyclopedic prose. Mitigation turns out to be cheap: in Italian, a one-line instruction cuts the figure by half to nearly three-quarters, and a supervised-fine-tuning adapter removes it almost entirely, with a scaling coefficient that can dial the reduction back onto the human rate. That last point is the author's actual target — calibration per genre, not elimination — and the closing worry is the reverse direction of influence: that we start writing like the machines. Boggia, arXiv 2026.

related.title: InstructGPT: Aligning LMs with Human Feedback (RLHF)
related.hook: A smaller model people actually like beats a bigger one they don't. InstructGPT used human preferences to make a model follow instructions — the recipe behind ChatGPT.

related.title: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)
related.hook: RLHF works but is fiddly: a separate reward model and a finicky RL loop. DPO reaches the same goal with one simple loss — and became a popular default.

related.title: Gotta Catch Them All: The Modes of Sycophancy
related.hook: Sycophancy looks like one behavior on the surface — but inside the model it splits into three distinct modes, perfectly separable from layer 14 on, each with its own circuitry.

related.title: Post-Training Shifts Confidence: SFT, RL, and OPD Shape Calibration Differently
related.hook: SFT, RL, and on-policy distillation all boost reasoning accuracy — but they leave completely different fingerprints on when a model's confidence signal can actually be trusted.

flashcards.prompt: What is epanorthosis, and what does it look like in LLM output?
flashcards.back_html: A classical figure of self-correction: reject a plain description, then substitute a grander one. The specimen the essay uses is "This is not a course. It is a journey of transformation."

flashcards.prompt: What does the essay identify as the main driver of the habit?

choices.text: A training distribution rich in promotional prose plus preference tuning that rewards confident, emphatic phrasing
Left-to-right generation, which forces the model to patch up sentences after committing to them
Tokenizer artifacts that make the construction unusually cheap to emit

flashcards.explanation_html: The author treats autoregressive generation as an amplifier rather than the root cause; the data distribution and RLHF's taste for emphasis do the real work.

flashcards.prompt: Why does the essay argue for calibration rather than eliminating the figure?
flashcards.back_html: Humans use epanorthosis too, at genre-specific rates — measurements found models overshooting in oratory but undershooting in informal Q&A. The target is the human rate per genre.
